summary: The only US national park south of the equator: rainforest ridges, coral reefs and white-sand beaches on three Samoan islands. The land is leased from village councils, and the park protects the Samoan way of life alongside the reef and the fruit bats.
story: The park is three pieces of three volcanic islands. On Tutuila it takes in the steep, forested ridge above Pago Pago Harbor and the north coast below it; on Ofu, a beach and the coral reef off the island's southeast shore; and on Taʻū, nearly two-thirds of the island, rising from the sea to Lata Mountain, at 3,170 feet the highest point in American Samoa. Roughly a third of the park's 8,257 acres is reef and ocean.

The park exists because of a bat. In the 1980s a campaign led by the ethnobotanist Paul Cox and local supporters set out to protect the old paleotropical rainforest and the Samoan flying fox, a fruit bat that pollinates and spreads its trees. The reefs turned out to be as remarkable as the forest: hundreds of species of fish and corals in shallow, clear water off Ofu.

Samoan people have lived on these islands for around three thousand years, and the park is unusual in protecting a living culture as well as a landscape. Under the communal land system the National Park Service cannot own the land, so it leases it: a fifty-year agreement with the village councils, signed in 1993, five years after Congress created the park. Fa'asamoa — the Samoan way — governs life in the villages the park surrounds.

In September 2009 an earthquake and tsunami struck the islands, killing 34 people and destroying the park's visitor center and offices. The park has rebuilt in Pago Pago, and remains one of the least visited in the system — a few tens of thousands of visits a year.

sights.name: Mount Alava
sights.note: The ridge-top trail above Pago Pago Harbor, with the harbor on one side and the north coast falling away on the other.

sights.name: Vatia and Pola Island
sights.note: A north-coast village beneath the ridge, facing the sheer sea stack of Pola Island.

sights.name: Ofu Beach
sights.note: A long white-sand beach on Ofu, with some of the clearest snorkelling in the territory over the reef.

sights.name: Saua
sights.note: A site on Taʻū that Samoan tradition holds sacred, below forested cliffs.

entrances: Tutuila: the visitor center is in Pago Pago, and the Mount Alava trail and the road to Vatia start nearby
Ofu and Taʻū: reached by small plane from Tutuila, on a limited schedule
lodging: No lodging inside the park; hotels and guesthouses around Pago Pago on Tutuila
seasonalClosures: Rain is possible at any time of year; tropical storms are most frequent from October to May

chronology.text: Delegate Fofō Sunia introduces a bill to protect the rainforest and the flying fox.
Congress establishes the National Park of American Samoa.
The Park Service signs a 50-year lease for the park's land with the village councils.
Congress approves an expansion of about thirty percent on Ofu and Olosega.
An earthquake and tsunami destroy the park's visitor center and offices.

safety: Currents over and beyond the reef can be strong. Snorkel inside the reef, in calm water, and never alone.
Trails are steep and slippery after rain, which is often. Carry water; the heat and humidity are constant.
regulations: Village land is not public land: ask permission before swimming, walking or taking photographs near a village, and keep Sundays quiet.
Corals, shells and other natural objects may not be taken.
Drones may not be launched, landed or flown in the park.
